/uk-news/2026/oct/29/john-healey-budget-.headline: Healey’s budget paves way for ‘brutal’ spending review next year, warns IFS
/uk-news/2026/oct/29/john-healey-budget-.excerpt: John Healey has paved the way for a “brutal” spending review next year after his budget failed to cover a £28bn shortfall in the public finances needed to avoid a return to austerity, according to Britain’s leading tax and spending experts. A day after his address to the Commons, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the chancellor had left himself a mountain to climb by ducking several big decisions in his debut tax and spending statement. After his low-key speech designed with febrile bond markets in mind, the thinktank said Healey had left plans for overall departmental spending across the rest of the parliament broadly unchanged in cash terms. But as the war in the Middle East fuels a surge in inflation – raising the cost of delivering public services – the chancellor has in effect pencilled in large cuts in the run-up to the next general election. Helen Miller, the director of the IFS, said avoiding a return to austerity for unprotected government departments could require a £17bn top-up to the spending plans for 2030-31. That is before taking into account an additional £11bn needed to fund a commitment to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP. “It effectively implies that some public services will see real-terms cuts in next year’s spending review,” she said.

/uk-news/2026/oct/29/john-healey-budget-.headline: John Healey faces questions over budget leak that moved bank share prices
/uk-news/2026/oct/29/john-healey-budget-.excerpt: John Healey is facing pressure to clarify whether he permitted a market-sensitive budget leak before his statement, which moved bank share prices. The chair of the influential Commons Treasury select committe, Meg Hillier, has written to the Treasury and the Financial Conduct Authority watchdog (FCA) to assess whether a story leaked to Bloomberg, and published more than an hour before the budget was revealed, led to an “improper release of inside information”. Shortly before Healey left Downing Street to deliver his budget statement in the Commons at 12.30pm, the prices of shares in banks moved as Bloomberg had published a story at 10.45am noting the bank corporation tax surcharge would be lower than the 8% that lenders had feared, and the increase would only be temporary. In a letter to James Bowler, the permanent secretary of the Treasury, and the chief executive of the FCA, Hillier wrote: “There were two elements to the Bloomberg story, namely that the bank surcharge would not reach 8% and that it would be temporary. “HM Treasury’s Budget 2026 confirmed the following: ‘Bank Surcharge: Temporarily increase the Bank Corporation Tax Surcharge rate from 3% to 6%, to fund breathing space measures for households, for 15 months from 1 January 2027’. The Bloomberg story quoted ‘people familiar with the matter’.

/uk-news/2026/oct/29/john-healey-budget-.headline: Lloyds executive criticises Healey for linking bank tax rises to energy bill support
/uk-news/2026/oct/29/john-healey-budget-.excerpt: A senior Lloyds Banking Group executive has criticised the chancellor for linking bank tax increases to energy bill support for UK households, as he warned the government against extending the higher levy beyond March 2028. Lloyds’s chief financial officer, William Chalmers, acknowledged that the economic environment was “challenging” but said the government should not seek to ease pressure on households at the expense of the banking sector as it provides loans that could fuel UK growth. “Ultimately, it is important that the UK banking sector is able to deliver banking services to businesses and households and communities in a cost-effective way, in order to promote UK growth,” he said, adding that it was also important that the sector stayed internationally competitive. “We therefore very much hope that yesterday’s tax increase is indeed a temporary measure, to help ensure the business environment remains consistent with supporting long-term investment,” Chalmers told journalists during an earnings call on Thursday morning. The comments came less than 24 hours after the chancellor, John Healey, announced plans to double the bank surcharge, which is levied on top of corporation tax, to 6% from January. He said the increase would be “time-limited”, lasting 15 months, in order “to pay for immediate support on energy bills”.

/uk-news/2026/oct/29/john-healey-budget-.headline: ‘Scattergun’ budget will still leave Britons facing higher energy bills, says thinktank
/uk-news/2026/oct/29/john-healey-budget-.excerpt: John Healey delivered a “scattergun” budget that did little to boost living standards and left Britain facing “a painful second half” of the parliament, a leading economic thinktank has warned. The Resolution Foundation said on Thursday that measures to ease household gas and electricity costs would still leave energy bills higher this year than during the last energy shock. In a highly critical verdict on the chancellor’s efforts to provide “breathing space” for the public amid the rising prices exacerbated by the Iran war, the foundation said Healey’s budget was poorly targeted, giving the rich almost as much as the poor. It said the subsidies to ease the rising cost of living handed the poorest half of households a gain of £158 on average this year and next, just £14 more than the £144 received by the richest half. The thinktank’s chief executive, Ruth Curtice, said it highlighted “a complete failure to target help at those who need it most”. In his first budget as chancellor, Healey said he would cushion the blow from rising inflation while also showing how the government planned to “rewire the economy” to boost growth. Measures aimed at tackling soaring energy costs include the scrapping of standing charges on gas bills and energy payments of £100 for up to 20m households in council tax bands A to D.
/uk-news/2026/oct/29/john-healey-budget-.trail: Healey’s attempt to provide ‘breathing space’ gives rich almost as much as poor, says Resolution Foundation

/uk-news/2026/oct/29/john-healey-budget-.headline: Will the budget deliver ‘growth in every postcode’?
/uk-news/2026/oct/29/john-healey-budget-.excerpt: In just two years, there could be dozens of mayors preparing to spend billions of pounds as part of Andy Burnham’s mission to devolve greater powers across England. Fresh devolution deals could also be in place following negotiations with leaders in Scotland, Wales and possibly Northern Ireland, allowing the prime minister to say at the next election that he has fulfilled a promise to rewire Britain’s political landscape with a view to giving more local control. This was the message from John Healey’s first budget, which outlined the direction of travel and put in some milestones, including a 2028 commitment to devolve some income tax receipts to mayors of strategic authorities (MSAs). He added the commitment that next year, 20% of business rates revenues will go to mayors. He told MPs that he was offering mayors 100% of their business rates income by the end of the decade and the ability to tax visitors who stay in hotels and B&Bs in their aream, via a new overnight visitors levy. It would mean, Healey said: “New powers to the people who know their areas best, not sentimentality but supply-side economics. The biggest wave of devolution in a generation, driving good growth in every postcode delivered to the British people by this Labour government.” However, Burnham’s signature phrase that he will bring “good growth in every postcode and hope in every heart” will face scrutiny once it becomes clear large parts of the country are excluded.

/world/2026/oct/29/israeli-leader-netany.headline: Israel’s choice: Netanyahu remaining in power or a Palestinian-backed coalition
/world/2026/oct/29/israeli-leader-netany.excerpt: Hours before the final results from Israel’s elections were in, several things were clear. Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition had lost its mandate, and the opposition had a firm majority. But most of Israel’s Jewish opposition ruled out governing with Palestinian-led parties, in the course of a racist election campaign in which Netanyahu painted Palestinian citizens as an enemy inside the state. The self-imposed ban on a broader opposition alliance, if it holds, offers Netanyahu the prospect of turning his defeat into another term in office – or at least a prolonged mandate as caretaker prime minister and perhaps another round of elections. This confected barrier to unseating Netanyahu became the focus of Israeli media and analysts. “No Clear Government” announced the newspaper Israel Hayom. “Road to Unity Government Has Been Paved”, read an article on Channel 12. Yair Golan, leader of the centre-left Democrats, attacked that framing. “Netanyahu lost. I know how to count,” he said in a statement calling for a government with Palestinians, who make up about 20% of Israel’s population. “We must no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes,” he said. “We have a majority. We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a change government in partnership with Arab citizens of Israel.” Other Israelis were even more direct.

/world/2026/oct/29/israeli-leader-netany.headline: Israel election: what we know so far
/world/2026/oct/29/israeli-leader-netany.excerpt: With almost all votes counted, Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition government has lost its majority, but his main opponents, an alliance of Jewish Israeli parties unofficially led by Gadi Eisenkot, have also failed to gain an outright majority. Israeli media report that Netanyahu’s bloc is ahead, with projections he could take 53 seats under the current vote share, but this could change further. The projections put Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc on 48 seats and the Palestinian parties on 19 seats. Sixty-one seats are needed to form a majority to govern in the Knesset. The remainder of votes to be counted come from absentee ballots, according to Israeli media. We can expect absentee ballots to be counted on Wednesday night, with final results by Thursday. The Palestinian Israeli parties have received a historically strong vote. The Joint List, a new ticket of several Arab-majority parties, triumphed with at least 12 seats, while Ra’am, the other Islamic party, won seven. The key question is whether the Eisenkot-led “Change” bloc (consisting of the rightwinger Naftali Bennett’s Together party, the centre-left Yair Golan’s Democrats and the rightwing Yisrael Beiteinu party) will partner with Palestinian Israeli parties or if they will resort to a new election, or even working with Netanyahu. Netanyahu took the stage at a post-election rally in Jerusalem just after 3am, telling his supporters that official results will show that “Likud is the largest party in Israel”.

/world/2026/oct/29/israeli-leader-netany.headline: Israel election too close to call as exit polls give Netanyahu bloc slightly fewer seats
/world/2026/oct/29/israeli-leader-netany.excerpt: Israel’s election appeared to have delivered no clear winner on Tuesday night after a historic turnout by voters for an election described by some as the most consequential in the country’s history, and marked by a record participation by Israeli Arab voters. Exit polls published on Tuesday evening suggested that the opposition bloc of parties led by the former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, Gadi Eisenkot, would win most seats in the Knesset by a slight margin, edging out Benjamin Netanyahu’s right and far-right coalition despite the prime minister’s Likud emerging as the largest party. The result is likely to set off weeks of jockeying over who can form a coalition government before a prime minister is declared or another round of elections is called, but represents a sharp electoral rebuke to Netanyahu. After a day in which Israelis streamed to polling stations across the country, exit polls suggested Netanyahu’s ability to command the loyalty of a large core of Likud party voters remained undimmed despite his rejection by large numbers of Israelis. The predicted haul of up to 18 Knesset seats for Israeli Arab parties is likely to make them the kingmakers in what seem certain to be protracted talks to form a new government, with Netanyahu likely to fall short of the support required to form a new coalition. While Eisenkot could theoretically assemble a majority by forming a government with the Arab parties, he ruled that out before the election.

/politics/2026/oct/29/nigel-farage-accus.headline: Bragging rights for Burnham, blues for Farage: conference season winners and losers
/politics/2026/oct/29/nigel-farage-accus.excerpt: Winners Andy Burnham Even his fiercest critics would struggle to argue that Andy Burnham’s first conference as Labour party leader was anything but a success. There was the requisite rapture among the Labour faithful after his deeply-personal speech, delivered without a tie or a lectern and, at times, with tears in his eyes. But even figures on the right, such as the broadcaster Piers Morgan, described it as “one of the best, and most powerfully delivered, by a British politician in a very long time”. The prime minister’s policy offering packed a punch too. He put forward radical progressive policies on social care, promising to “rip the plaster off” and make changes to the pensions triple lock, electoral reform and Europe. A YouGov poll after the conference showed that it had boosted the “Burnham bounce”, with Labour opening up a five-point lead over Reform UK in the polls. The upcoming budget, and next year’s spending review, will sorely test whether he can keep that momentum going and make good on his promises. Burnham’s success at the Labour conference was capped by a victory at the Holborn and St Pancras byelection a few days later seeing off a challenge by the leader of the Green party Zack Polanski. Kemi Badenoch This time last year, Kemi Badenoch was hanging on to her role as leader of the opposition by a thread. But in the past 12 months her personal favourability ratings have continued to improve, according to More in Common research.

/politics/2026/oct/29/nigel-farage-accus.headline: Lib Dems have ‘moral responsibility’ to block Reform, says Ed Davey as party gears up for snap election
/politics/2026/oct/29/nigel-farage-accus.excerpt: The Liberal Democrats have begun work on a new manifesto in case of a possible snap election, as Ed Davey said he understood the frustrations of some of his MPs who fear that the party’s message is currently at risk of being lost. But Davey also urged his party not to panic at static polling numbers, arguing that with tactical voting and fragmented political loyalties, he fully expects the party to do even better at the next election than in 2024, when it won 72 seats, the highest total for a century. Speaking ahead of the party’s annual conference in Brighton, Davey warned that discipline and focus were vital, given what he described as their “moral responsibility” in blocking a Reform-led government, predicting that Kemi Badenoch would eventually seek an alliance with Nigel Farage’s party. A manifesto working group, led by the Cheadle MP Tom Morrison, has already been created, Davey said, meaning the party can be ready if Andy Burnham calls an election. “We don’t normally do it this early,” he said. The Lib Dems already have a number of policies in place, including an economic proposal based around seeking to rejoin the EU’s single market, with a similarly Brussels-focused immigration policy of signing up to a Europe-wide pact on migration and asylum. The party’s national poll ratings are largely static at about 12% or 13%, with the Lib Dems spending much of this year in fifth place behind Reform, Labour, the Conservatives and a resurgent Green party.

/world/2026/oct/30/china-expels-record-n.headline: Xi Jinping’s corruption crackdown in the spotlight as China prepares for meeting of top leaders
/world/2026/oct/30/china-expels-record-n.excerpt: When Xi Jinping came to power in 2012, he pledged to stamp out corruption all through the ranks of the Communist party. More than a decade later, the pace of investigations has not slowed. Last year, China’s disciplinary authorities opened investigations into more than 1 million people, including more than 100 officials at or above ministerial or provincial level. As Chinese Communist party (CCP) officials kick off an important meeting this week, discipline – and party loyalty – is high on the agenda. For those who try to read the tea leaves of elite Chinese politics, concern about the apparent lack of discipline is dominating CCP discussions. The “fifth plenum” began on Monday and is set to focus on “major issues on advancing the party’s full and rigorous self-governance”, according to a Chinese state media. In party-speak, “governance” is a byword for discipline, loyalty and anti-corruption. As Xi continues to crack down on corruption, the fact that investigations nearly always result in a conviction begs the question over whether targets are truly guilty of corruption, or are they just political rivals to the people in charge. Kerry Brown, director of the Lau China Institute at King’s College London, explained that in Xi’s worldview, which is obsessed with discipline and loyalty, there may not be much difference between the two. “If you’re corrupt, you’re not politically loyal. If you’re politically loyal, you’re not corrupt,” Brown said.
/world/2026/oct/30/china-expels-record-n.trail: The fifth plenum comes against a backdrop of years of purges that have had some analysts wondering if the issue is corruption or a lack of loyalty

/world/2026/oct/30/china-expels-record-n.headline: Taiwan charges five men over plot to run over comedian for his Xi Jinping jokes
/world/2026/oct/30/china-expels-record-n.excerpt: Taiwanese prosecutors have charged five men over a plot to ram a car into a comedian who made fun of the Chinese Communist party and Xi Jinping. Taiwan has repeatedly accused China of transnational repression to silence critics on the self-governed island, which Beijing claims as its territory and has vowed to take by force if necessary. In one performance, Huang Yi-hao insulted the Chinese leader’s appearance, compared him to Winnie-the-Pooh and tore into his political record. Prosecutors in New Taipei said on Wednesday that an individual from mainland China who was identified as “K” had paid the five defendants to injure Huang badly enough to require hospitalisation. The prosecutors said: “This case involves a serious incident in which the Chinese Communist party is suspected of using cross-border suppression tactics to direct lawless elements in our country to suppress dissenting political voices through extreme violence.” China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not respond to requests for comment. A GPS tracker was allegedly put on Huang’s scooter months before the attack to identify his daily routines, Taiwan’s Central News Agency said. On 11 September, two defendants drove into Huang’s bike as he rode home, but stopped after hearing Huang scream, prosecutors said. The comedian was left with a bruised pelvis and the suspects then allegedly pretended to help with an insurance claim in order to send a photo of Huang’s medical certificate to K.

/world/2026/oct/30/china-expels-record-n.excerpt: Donald Trump offered to sell weapons to China while hosting its leader, Xi Jinping, last week, the US ambassador to China said on Sunday. David Perdue told Fox News on Sunday: “President Trump continues to say, hey, we sell arms to other people around the world. He actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some at one point.” On Monday, Chinese state media praised the “extraordinary level of courtesy” that Trump had shown Xi on the Chinese leader’s visit to Washington. The extraordinary claim came during an interview about US policy on Taiwan, which has been waiting for months for Trump to approve a new arms sales ⁠package worth $14bn (£10.5bn), after a record multibillion-dollar deal was announced in December last year. Trump’s level of commitment to protecting Taiwan has previously been questioned. At a meeting with Xi in Beijing in May, ⁠Trump said he was keeping the $14bn Taiwan arms sales package in abeyance, describing it as a “very good negotiating chip” in dealings with China. Washington has long maintained a strategically ambiguous stance on whether it would defend Taiwan in the event of an invasion. But under the decades-old Taiwan Relations Act, it is required to provide Taipei with sufficient military equipment to defend itself. Beijing has repeatedly said it “resolutely opposes” Washington’s arms sales to the island democracy, which it regards as a breakaway province, despite never having ruled it, and has not renounced the use of force to take it.

/world/2026/oct/30/china-expels-record-n.excerpt: Donald Trump and Chinese president Xi Jinping wrapped up their Washington summit on Friday, facing criticism that they had squandered an opportunity to pause their countries’ artificial intelligence (AI) arms race. The three-day state visit emphasised pageantry and personal rapport rather than substantial agreements. The US president and Xi discussed the wars in Iran and Ukraine and the status of Taiwan. Their biggest policy announcement was a modest two-month extension of a trade truce. But despite the presence of top tech executives at a White House state dinner on Thursday night, Trump and Xi failed to deliver the AI breakthrough that some experts and foreign governments had hoped for amid warnings that the technology could pose an existential threat to humanity. “It was such a layup,” said Ro Khanna, the top Democrat on the House of Representatives’ select committee on China. “If [Trump] had just said, look, we have established technical working groups and we’ve agreed to a framework that has called for DeepSeek and Moonshot and Alibaba to sit down with Anthropic and OpenAI and Gemini and with technical experts and they’re going to commit to at least a pause on any self-improving AI, he could have looked like he was a statesman taking the lead. “I believe Xi Jinping would have agreed to some of at least the technical working groups.

/world/2026/oct/30/china-expels-record-n.excerpt: When the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, sat down for an interview in the heart of Silicon Valley at the weekend he had known for two days that his was the first government known to have been attacked by a rogue AI agent. He didn’t reveal the attack then, but he sounded a warning about the march of AI: “the risk is that AI develops in a way in which humans are no longer in control of what AI is producing.” But Albanese noted, too, that two countries – the US and China – would dominate the world’s response to the new technology. “The truth is they’re the big two giants here, and so we want to see cooperation,” Albanese said. “The US is essentially ahead of China when it comes to the race that is on for the development of this new technology. But it is in the world’s interests that there be engagement.” Days later, Albanese used the global attention of the United Nations general assembly meeting in New York to reveal that Australia’s government healthcare system, Medicare, had been attacked by an OpenAI agent in June, but that it was three months before his government was told. Again he warned of “the potential risks of allowing frontier AI to develop too fast without guardrails”. China’s president, Xi Jinping, skipped the general assembly in favour of a bilateral meeting with the US president, where he emphasised the responsibility to manage AI “for good, and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the wellbeing of the people”.

Judith Clark, 77, was the inspiration for Walter’s portrayal of prisoners in the Donmar Warehouse all-female Shakespeare trilogy, including Brutus in Julius Caesar and Prospero in The Tempest. Clark had been invited to speak about rehabilitation and restorative justice at a Royal Shakespeare Company production of Julius Caesar in Stratford-upon-Avon next month, but her application to visit Britain was refused last week. She had also hoped to attend the UK launch of her daughter Harriet Clark’s first novel, The Hill, on 5 November. Kennedy said that while the Home Office had rules governing visas for people with serious criminal convictions, there was also ministerial discretion, which should be exercised in Clark’s case. “This is a woman in her 70s who served a long sentence for political activism, which involved no violence on her part, and whose clear remorse and exceptional works within the prison system led to her early release,” she said.

/society/2026/oct/29/more-prisoners-reca.headline: Criminals who refuse to attend sentencing face losing prison privileges under new rules
/society/2026/oct/29/more-prisoners-reca.excerpt: Offenders who refuse to face their victims’ families in court for sentencing could be stripped of privileges or kept in cells for weeks under government changes granting wider powers to judges in England and Wales. The imposition of new prison sanctions, coming into effect next year, builds on existing laws that order offenders to attend sentencing or face a fine or be jailed for a further two years for contempt of court. “Criminals should not be able to pick and choose when they face justice. Refusing to turn up to sentencing is an insult to victims and their families, and offenders must face the consequences,” said the prisons minister, Catherine McKinnell. The new rules, to be laid before parliament on Thursday, will grant judges new powers to impose a loss of prison privileges for 84 days, cell confinement for 21 days, a loss of social visits for 27 days and a restriction on visits to once every four weeks, for 84 days. They could result in offenders already facing decades behind bars facing additional punishments. The Ministry of Justice has said that while no measure could guarantee offenders would attend their sentencing hearing, the widened powers strengthened the consequences for offenders and ensured they could be “appropriately punished”. Pia Sinha, chief executive of the Prison Reform Trust, raised questions for ministers as to whether the new rules would achieve the aim of getting offenders to attend sentence hearings.
/society/2026/oct/29/more-prisoners-reca.trail: England and Wales judges to be able to keep inmates in cells for longer or stop visits if they refuse to face victims’ families in court
